keywords: crypto tax software vs qualified appraisal

mainEntity.name: What is a qualified appraisal for digital assets under IRS rules?

acceptedAnswer.text: A qualified appraisal is a formal valuation of digital assets conducted by a qualified appraiser in accordance with generally accepted appraisal standards (USPAP), as defined by IRC §170(f)(11)(E)(i). It requires a detailed property description, FMV determination with documented methodology, appraiser certification and qualification disclosure, and independence from the taxpayer and transaction.

mainEntity.name: Does crypto tax software produce a qualified appraisal?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Crypto tax software platforms (CoinTracker, CoinLedger, Koinly, TaxBit) produce tax preparation reports for cost basis and gain/loss calculations, but they do not produce qualified appraisals. An algorithm cannot satisfy the qualified appraiser requirements of IRC §170(f)(11)(E), and automated price feeds do not constitute USPAP-compliant valuation methodology.

mainEntity.name: What qualifications must a digital asset appraiser have?

acceptedAnswer.text: Under IRC §170(f)(11)(E)(ii)-(iii), a qualified appraiser must: (1) hold a professional designation from a recognized appraisal organization or meet minimum education and experience requirements; (2) regularly perform appraisals for compensation; (3) demonstrate verifiable education and experience in valuing the specific type of property (digital assets); and (4) not have been prohibited from IRS practice under Circular 230 within the prior three years.

mainEntity.name: What is the $5,000 threshold for qualified appraisals?

acceptedAnswer.text: IRC §170(f)(11)(C) requires a qualified appraisal for any property contribution for which a deduction exceeding $5,000 is claimed. Under aggregation rules (§170(f)(11)(F)), similar items of property donated to one or more donees are treated as a single property — meaning multiple digital asset donations in a tax year are aggregated for threshold purposes.

mainEntity.name: What penalties apply for not obtaining a qualified appraisal?

acceptedAnswer.text: Without a qualified appraisal, the taxpayer risks: (1) denial of the charitable deduction; (2) accuracy-related penalties of 20% under IRC §6662 for negligence or substantial valuation misstatement; (3) penalties of 40% for gross valuation misstatements (claimed value >200% of correct value); (4) indefinite statute of limitations for gift tax purposes under Treas. Reg. §301.6501(c)-1(f); and (5) interest on all underpayments from the original due date.

mainEntity.name: Can I use an exchange price as my crypto valuation for IRS purposes?

acceptedAnswer.text: For routine cost basis and gain/loss reporting on Form 1099-DA, exchange transaction prices are generally acceptable. However, for any purpose requiring substantiation of FMV — charitable donations, gift tax reporting, estate tax filings, trust funding, IRA valuations — an exchange price alone does not constitute a qualified appraisal. The IRS has explicitly stated in CCA 202302012 that exchange-reported values do not substitute for qualified appraisals.

mainEntity.name: What is USPAP and why does it matter for crypto appraisals?

acceptedAnswer.text: USPAP (Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice) is the generally accepted appraisal standards recognized by the Treasury Department under IRC §170(f)(11)(E)(i)(II). For digital assets, USPAP Standard 7 governs the development of personal property appraisals and Standard 8 governs their reporting. The Appraisal Foundation, the certifying organization, mandates that appraisers complete annual USPAP continuing education to maintain their credentials.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between a qualified appraisal and a crypto tax report?

acceptedAnswer.text: A crypto tax report calculates cost basis and capital gains/losses for income tax purposes, using transaction-level data and historical pricing. A qualified appraisal provides a professional opinion of fair market value for substantiation purposes, following USPAP methodology, signed by a qualified appraiser under IRC §170(f)(11)(E). They serve complementary but distinct functions: the tax report supports income tax compliance; the qualified appraisal supports FMV substantiation for deductions, gifts, and estate reporting.
